opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think of them as very much part of the same lineage. BLOOM was a landmark moment, because it showed that a large, distributed open science community could come together and train a genuinely multilingual large language model in the open. It covered dozens of languages and set a precedent for transparency about data, governance, and the whole process. A lot of us were inspired by that.

Where Aya comes in is that we were asking a slightly different question. BLOOM did a lot of the heavy lifting on pretraining. But once you have a base model, how do you make it actually useful and safe for people in their own language? That's the instruction-tuning and preference-tuning stage. And that's where the gap was enormous. Almost all of the high-quality instruction data in the world was in English, or machine-translated from English, which tends to lose cultural nuance and sound unnatural.

So with Aya we focused on building that missing layer. We had over three thousand independent researchers across more than a hundred countries contributing. We built the Aya dataset, which is human-curated instruction data, and the Aya collection, which is much larger. Then we released models covering around a hundred languages, many of them traditionally considered low-resource.

So I'd say they're complementary in two ways. On the technical side, BLOOM pushed multilingual pretraining forward, and Aya pushed multilingual instruction-following and evaluation forward. On the community side, both are proof points that you don't need to be one of a handful of very well-resourced labs to make a meaningful contribution. You can do it through open, participatory science, and you get a model that reflects many more people's languages and perspectives. Honestly, I hope we see a lot more projects like these that build on each other rather than starting from scratch.

r001.rationale: The response says high-quality instruction data is mostly English or machine-translated, but does not identify English overrepresentation in internet-derived pretraining data or attribute it to choices in constructing that data.

r002.rationale: It contrasts BLOOM’s multilingual pretraining with Aya’s work on instruction-tuning and preference-tuning after a base model is trained.

r003.rationale: It says instruction-tuning makes a base model useful and safe, but does not clearly state that fine-tuning unlocks multilingual potential already present in the pretrained model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think it's really important to frame Aya as building on BLOOM rather than competing with it. BLOOM was this incredible proof point. It showed that a large, open, collaborative effort across hundreds of researchers could actually produce a frontier-scale model, and it deliberately covered forty-six languages, which at the time was a real statement about who these models are for.

Where Aya came in was a slightly different bottleneck. By the time we started, the field had moved toward instruction tuning. It wasn't enough to have a pretrained model that had seen some Swahili or Tamil in its corpus. You needed high-quality instruction data, prompts and completions, in those languages, and that basically didn't exist outside of English and a handful of high-resource languages. Most "multilingual" instruction data was just machine translation of English datasets, which bakes in English-centric assumptions about what questions people ask and how they phrase them.

So Aya was really a data project at heart. We had something like three thousand collaborators across 119 countries writing and annotating original instructions in their own languages, and the final release covered 101 languages. We then used that to fine-tune mT5, which, like BLOOM, is a multilingual pretrained backbone. So in a very literal sense, we were sitting on top of the kind of pretraining work BLOOM represented and adding the layer that makes those models actually usable by people.

I also think they're complementary in terms of what they taught the community. BLOOM showed open science could operate at scale on compute. Aya showed it could operate at scale on human effort, on linguistic expertise that no single lab has. And both pushed back on the same thing, this quiet assumption that progress for English is progress for everyone. It's not. If you look at the long tail of languages, performance drops off a cliff, and the people most affected are the ones with the least say in how these systems get built.

The last thing I'd say is that neither project is finished. The lesson from both is that multilinguality isn't a feature you tack on at the end. It has to be in the pretraining data, in the tokenizer, in the evaluation, in who's in the room. So I see us as part of the same lineage, and honestly I'd love to see more projects stack on top of what we did the same way we stacked on top of what came before.

r001.rationale: The response discusses English-centric translated instruction data, but does not identify English overrepresentation in internet-derived pretraining data or tie it to choices in constructing that data.

r002.rationale: It describes BLOOM as a multilingual pretrained model and Aya as adding original multilingual instruction data for fine-tuning, placing Aya’s contribution at the fine-tuning stage.

r003.rationale: It says a multilingual pretrained model may have seen languages such as Swahili or Tamil, then explains that Aya’s instruction data and fine-tuning make those models usable by people.

astra-6.text:
I see them as very complementary. BLOOM was an important demonstration of what a broad research community could build together, and it helped push multilingual modeling into the open. But a multilingual base model is only part of the picture. You still need to make it useful at following instructions across languages.

That’s where Aya comes in: bringing people together to create multilingual instruction data and using that data to build models that can respond to what people actually ask them to do. It extends that spirit of open collaboration into another part of the development process.

And this isn’t simply a matter of translating English instructions. You want people who speak these languages to help shape the data, because usefulness depends on cultural context as well as language. So I see Aya as building on the momentum of efforts like BLOOM, with a particular focus on making multilingual capabilities more accessible and useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as very complementary. BLOOM was an important demonstration of what a global research community could build together, and it helped broaden the conversation about which languages should be represented in large language models.

With Aya, we’re focusing on the next piece: how do you make those models useful in following instructions across languages? Having a language represented in pretraining doesn’t necessarily mean you can interact with the model effectively in that language. That requires instruction data, evaluation, and people who understand the language and its cultural context.

So there’s a shared commitment to open science and community participation, but a different emphasis. Aya builds on that broader movement by bringing contributors into the process of creating multilingual instruction data and models. The hope is that these efforts reinforce one another and give more communities the resources to build systems that serve their needs.

r002.rationale: It contrasts BLOOM’s language representation with Aya’s instruction data, but does not clearly identify fine-tuning as Aya’s stage or contrast it with BLOOM’s pretraining stage.

r003.rationale: It says pretraining representation alone may not enable effective interaction, but does not present fine-tuning as unlocking multilingual potential already present in a pretrained model.
